bio.en: Shweta Shrivastava is Senior Director of Product Management at Waymo, the self-driving car company, and previously held product leadership roles at Amazon and Cisco.
bio.zh: Shweta Shrivastava 是自动驾驶公司 Waymo 的产品管理高级总监，此前曾在 Amazon 和 Cisco 担任产品领导职务。

summary.en: Shweta shares product lessons from building autonomous vehicles, including how Waymo creates human-like driving behaviors and treats safety as the foundational product principle. She covers key lessons from her career at Amazon, Cisco, and startups about customer-centric product management, and why listening and empathy are core PM skills in complex technical environments. The episode is a fascinating look at product management inside one of the most advanced AI deployments on the roads today.
summary.zh: Shweta 分享了打造自动驾驶汽车的产品经验，包括 Waymo 如何创造类人的驾驶行为、并将安全视为基础性的产品原则。她讲到了在 Amazon、Cisco 以及初创公司生涯中关于“以客户为中心的产品管理”的关键心得，以及为什么在复杂技术环境中，倾听与同理心是产品经理的核心技能。本期是对当今道路上最先进 AI 部署之一内部产品管理的精彩透视。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's great to have you. I thought we'd start with just a little bit about what it is you do at Waymo today. What are you and your team's responsible for at Waymo?
turns.zh: 很高兴您能加入我们。首先，我想请您简单介绍一下您目前在Waymo的职责。您和您的团队在Waymo负责哪些方面的工作？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yes, my team's responsible for three key areas, I would say. One is building a big part of the software that actually runs on board the fully autonomous vehicle and that determines the actual behavior and trajectory of the vehicle. Secondly, building the simulation tools and technologies that are required to validate the performance of the system. And then, a third one of the teams focused on commercially scaling our ride-hailing business, which is one of our key go-to market applications for the technology we're building.
turns.zh: 是的，我的团队主要负责三个关键领域。首先是开发用于全自动驾驶车辆的核心软件，决定车辆的实际行为和行驶路径。其次是构建验证系统性能所需的模拟工具和技术。第三个团队专注于商业化扩展我们的网约车业务，这是我们所开发技术的主要市场应用之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So as you know, I arranged a ride for me in a Waymo in San Francisco. It was actually a really rainy day and it was quite mind blowing. I've never been in a self-driving car that had no driver sitting in the front. I have a Tesla and I turn on self-driving sometimes, but I've never experienced just sitting in the back and this thing just raises you around. Also, just like a memory hat is the app to call the Waymo, it feels like Google Maps except instead of just telling you how to get to a place like a car shows up and just takes you there and then you could change course as you're driving and it's crazy how quickly it became normal. (05:08): I'm just like, all right, we're just riding around San Francisco in this self-driving car and just sitting in the back and telling you where to go. And so anyway, I'm going to ask you a bunch of questions around this, but I guess thank you for arranging that ride. It was quite special.
turns.zh: 正如您所知，我在旧金山乘坐了Waymo的自动驾驶车。那天雨下得很大，但体验令人惊叹。我从未乘坐过前排没有司机的自动驾驶汽车。我有一辆特斯拉，有时会开启自动驾驶模式，但从未体验过坐在后排让车辆自动接送的感觉。此外，呼叫Waymo的应用程序就像谷歌地图一样，只不过不是指路，而是车辆会主动接送你，而且在行驶过程中还能调整路线，这一切转变得如此自然，真是令人惊叹。（05:08）我当时就想，嗯，我们现在就坐在旧金山的自动驾驶车里，坐在后排让车辆带我们去目的地。所以，无论如何，我会围绕这些问题向您提问，但还是要感谢您安排这次体验。这真是特别的经历。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: No, I'm glad that you were able to do that on a rainy day. So that's a special bonus because, again, the technology has been performing very well, which has been very heartening for us to see.
turns.zh: 不，我很高兴您能在雨天体验到这种服务。这真是个额外惊喜，因为技术一直表现得非常出色，这让我们倍感欣慰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A few questions along these lines, one thing that I noticed that was really cool is we're trying to turn into a lane and there's cars coming in that lane just continuing to move and the car just kind of subtly was inching its way out, communicating through this interesting body language thing of just like, can someone let me in? And it's interesting, there's no eye contact involved and it's just like this, I don't know, gesture that you all have to develop. (05:54): And so, I guess, the question here is just like what have you all learned? And I don't know if you even work on that piece of it, but just, I'm curious how you think about creating this body language of the car communication system to help people understand what it's trying to do.
turns.zh: 接下来有几个相关问题。有一个我觉得特别酷的场景是，我们想变道时，旁边车道的车辆继续行驶，而我们的车会悄悄地挪出空位，靠一种有趣的肢体语言来示意“能让一下吗？”有趣的是，这里没有眼神交流，全靠一种特定的手势来传达意思。（05:54）所以，我想问一下，大家从中获得了哪些启发？我不知道你们是否负责这部分工作，但我很好奇，你们如何设计这种车辆沟通的肢体语言，让人们理解车辆的意图？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: We're using a lot of human driving data to train our deep models. So it's important to make sure that the behavior of the car doesn't seem robotic, it can feel quite unnatural. And from the get-go, we focused on building a fully autonomous system. So it's important to have that familiarity, that trust, building with the riders where they're not daunted by technology, they don't feel like they're sitting in our walk. It has to feel very human-like, but in a good way. Making it safer than human driving, but then not making it feel unnatural. (06:40): And so we have deep learned models that can understand what the other road users' intent is. So, stuff like which way the pedestrian is looking or what is their body orientation because that could tell you which way they're headed. The road signs or the gestures, somebody is trying to stop the vehicle. The system can understand all those signals. (07:04): So because we're using deep learn models trained on human driving, but again sort of in a good way. We discard the bad human driving data. We can mimic human driving behavior in a good way and that's why you saw the behavior that you saw yesterday. Now, one thing to note is we can't also just completely rely on explicit gestures and signs because a lot of driving has also social norms. If you're in a pretty clear section in San Francisco, maybe it's okay for pedestrians to cross even when they don't have a walk sign. (07:43): Another city, another intersection might have a different social norm when it comes to pedestrians crossing the four-way stop sign or the crosswalk or what have you. And so, the car also has to learn about those social norms and be able to react to it. So, like I said, we don't realize how sophisticated, how interactive and how social driving really is. And with our artificial intelligence capabilities, we have been able to incorporate a lot of that into our system behavior.
turns.zh:
我们正在利用大量人类驾驶数据来训练我们的深度学习模型。因此，确保汽车的行为不显得机械化至关重要，否则会显得非常不自然。从一开始，我们就致力于打造一个完全自动驾驶的系统。因此，与乘客建立熟悉感和信任感非常重要，让他们不被技术吓倒，也不会觉得自己是在被动接受服务。这必须让人感觉非常人性化，但要以积极的方式实现。让它比人类驾驶更安全，同时又不显得生硬。（06:40）  
  我们拥有深度学习模型，能够理解其他道路使用者的意图。比如，观察行人看向哪个方向，或者他们的身体姿态，因为这些信息能揭示他们的行进方向。道路标志或手势，比如有人试图阻止车辆前进。系统能够理解所有这些信号。（07:04）  
  由于我们使用的是基于人类驾驶数据训练的深度学习模型，但还是以积极的方式进行优化。我们会剔除不良的人类驾驶数据，模仿人类的驾驶行为，这就是你昨天看到的那些表现。  
  需要注意的是，我们不能完全依赖明确的手势和信号，因为许多驾驶行为都受社会规范约束。比如在旧金山的某些路段，即使没有行人过街信号，行人过马路也可能是被允许的。而在其他城市，红绿灯或人行横道的社会规范可能截然不同。因此，汽车还必须学习这些社会规范，并能够做出相应的反应。正如我所说，我们没有意识到驾驶行为实际上是多么复杂、互动性强且具有社会性的。凭借我们的人工智能能力，我们已经能够将许多这些特性融入到我们的系统行为中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So before Waymo, you worked at non self-driving software companies, you worked at Amazon, Cisco, a few other companies. I'm curious what you've found to be the biggest difference working in a company like Waymo versus a traditional software company.
turns.zh: 在加入Waymo之前，你曾在非自动驾驶软件公司工作，比如亚马逊、思科等公司。我很好奇，与传统软件公司相比，在Waymo这样的公司工作最大的不同之处是什么？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: As I said earlier, it's a highly complex, technically complex, system that we have built and we're improving. And if I may say, it's the most game changing product that anybody would ever work on.
turns.zh: 正如我之前所说，我们构建并持续改进的是一个高度复杂、技术难度极高的系统。如果我可以这么说的话，这是任何人有机会参与的最具变革性的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know, Amazon's pretty cool, but I totally get you.
turns.zh: 我不知道，亚马逊确实很酷，但我完全理解你的感受。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I worked at Amazon, I'm a fan. And they have been pretty transformational with AWS and on the eCommerce side. But a fully autonomous driving system, it's also a very, very hard problem. So it's transformational from that perspective too. I would say that the PMC has to be able to go technically indeed, compared to what they would do in other software products. They have to be able to get into the details as much as needed. They have to be okay with uncertainty and ambiguity. (09:24): Again, I think, that is part and parcel of any product management role, but it's even more so here. This is a long game and so you have to have the tenacity to play the long game and be continuously improving the product and make this thing a broad reality and future. So, those are some of the attributes. I would also say that there is some level of self selection here. You have to be driven by the mission to make the roads safer. We have about 1.35 million debts that happen every year across the world from traffic accidents and most of that is attributable to driving errors and driver distraction. (10:04): I've been guilty of checking my text messages while driving. I've seen other drivers do that. But a fully autonomous technology, you don't have that risk. That's the risk we're trying to minimize. So they have to be driven by that mission. One other thing is that the concept of MVP, which is so widely popular in the SaaS product management world or product management world, in general, has a whole new meaning here at Waymo when you work in a product like this because safety is on top of mind for all of us and can't really cut corners on safety. (10:42): The MVP bar itself for safety is extremely high for us. So, the core product management philosophy also, getting an MVP out there and then iterating with the real world deployment. It applies, but it's just a different bar on that MVP.
turns.zh:
我曾在亚马逊工作过，是亚马逊的粉丝。他们在AWS和电商领域确实带来了深刻的变革。但完全自动驾驶系统同样是一个极其困难的挑战。从这个角度来看，它同样具有变革意义。我认为产品管理总监必须具备扎实的技术能力，这与其他软件产品的要求相比要高得多。他们必须能够深入了解技术细节，坦然面对不确定性和模糊性。

（09:24）：再说一次，我认为这是任何产品管理角色的基本要求，但在这里显得尤为重要。这是一场持久战，因此你必须具备持之以恒的耐力，持续改进产品，让这项技术真正成为现实并造福未来。这就是产品管理的核心素养之一。此外，这里还存在一定的自我筛选机制。你必须被让道路更安全的使命所驱动。全球每年有约135万起交通事故，其中大部分源于驾驶失误和司机分心。

（10:04）：我自己就曾在开车时查看过短信，也见过其他司机这样做。但完全自动驾驶技术就不会存在这种风险。这正是我们努力降低的风险。因此，他们必须被这一使命所驱动。此外，MVP（最小可行产品）概念在SaaS产品管理领域或一般产品管理中广为人知，但在Waymo这样的产品中，它有着全新的含义，因为安全是我们所有人最关心的头等大事，在安全问题上绝不能偷工减料。

（10:42）：对我们来说，MVP在安全方面的标准极其高。因此，核心的产品管理理念——先推出MVP，然后根据实际部署情况进行迭代——依然适用，但MVP的标准却截然不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Touching again on safety and human behavior, I was thinking a little bit as we're chatting about, say of Tesla, which has self-driving car, self-driving capabilities and intellectually I know it's probably going to drive a lot better than I am, but I still feel like I need to disengage it occasionally when I'm on a curvy road. I'm just like, I don't know about this, I don't want to leave room for error if there's something that weird that happens. (11:30): And I imagine someone designing product for that weird behavior where I should probably trust it because it's probably a lot better driver than I am, but I don't know, I feel like I can do a better job. Is there anything you've learned about, I don't know, human behavior or how to design software for these sorts of experiences that maybe surprised you or thought was really interesting or that was really important?
turns.zh:
再谈谈安全和人类行为。我在和大家聊天时想到，比如特斯拉，它有自动驾驶功能，从理性上讲，我知道它可能比我开车技术好得多，但在蜿蜒的道路上，我还是会偶尔接管驾驶权。我就想，我不太放心万一出现什么异常情况该怎么办。

（11:30）：我能想象产品经理在设计应对这种异常情况时，可能得让用户相信自动驾驶系统比自己强得多，但我还是会觉得自己能做得更好。有没有什么关于人类行为或如何为这类体验设计软件的经验，让你感到惊讶、觉得很有趣或非常重要？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Since you mentioned Tesla, I just want to clarify that it's a different system that we are building, which is for Waymo, we started by solving the problem of fully autonomous driving without a human driver at the wheel from the get-go. It's not a driver assist or aid system which relies on the human driver taking over when there's a complex situation. So I think that expectation is built into that kind of a product and so the human folks who are using that product will also have that mindset that, hey, I should be ready to take over when the situation demands because we've built the system from the get-go to work in a fully autonomous mode without a human driver intervention at the wheel. (12:38): We had to integrate this into our design philosophy from the very beginning that this has to feel credible, predictable and the writers have to be able to trust the system. So that has been sort of the core of the design philosophy. And so, what happens is, and I heard this from you as well, which resonated with me and I've heard this from a lot of our writers, that for the first five minutes of the ride it's, wow, is this thing really happening. (13:10): But then it starts to feel very natural and as if this is how it was always meant to be. After the first five minutes, this is like uneventful. That's exactly how it's supposed to feel, but it's not a happenstance that it feels that way. The naturalness, the smoothness and still adhering to safety at all times are things that are designed into the system. And then we make sure that the rider has visibility into what's happening. If they're not wearing the seatbelt, the rider support would call them. So then they know, okay, there's a human that they can reach out to if they have an issue. They can look at the monitor in the car to understand what the car is seeing. So I think all these little things help develop that trust in the system.
turns.zh:
既然你提到了特斯拉，我想说明一下，我们正在开发的系统与特斯拉的不同。我们从一开始就致力于解决完全自动驾驶的问题——即无需人类驾驶员即可实现全自动驾驶。这并非依赖于人类驾驶员在复杂情况下接管的辅助驾驶系统。因此，用户对该产品的期望已被内置于产品设计之中，使用该产品的驾驶员也会形成这样的心理预期：当情况需要时，他们必须随时准备接管控制权，因为我们从一开始就设计了系统，使其能够在无需人类干预的情况下实现全自动驾驶模式。  
（12:38）：我们必须从一开始就将这一理念融入设计哲学，即系统必须可信、可预测，驾驶员必须能够信任它。这始终是设计理念的核心。正如我从你们这里听到的，也与许多用户反馈一致，在乘车前五分钟，用户会惊叹“这真的能实现吗？”  
（13:10）：但随后用户会逐渐适应，觉得一切顺其自然，仿佛这就是应有的体验。过了五分钟，整个过程平静无波。这正是我们期望达到的效果，但这种自然流畅感并非偶然——安全性是系统设计的核心。我们还确保乘客能随时掌握车内动态。若乘客未系安全带，系统会发出提醒，让他们知道在遇到问题时可以联系到人工客服。他们可以通过车载显示屏了解车辆的感知信息。所有这些细节都有助于建立对系统的信任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that same note, what's one thing that your teams have built that creates a lot of trust or maybe it was a surprisingly important element in creating trust in the experience in terms of the product, especially in, I don't know, either the app or in car experience.
turns.zh: 同样，在产品设计方面，尤其是应用程序或车载体验中，有哪些关键设计细节能有效建立用户信任？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I don't know if I can point to one thing. Again, this is such a holistic experience that I think it has to be a bunch of small things to make it feel natural, transparent and trustworthy to the writers. And I can give you one example that I don't think I've mentioned in the discussion so far. So, again, because the system is designed to be cautious and defensive but still making adequate progress in the absence of traffic, it will never go above the speed limit. It doesn't go above the speed limit. It sticks or adheres to the speed limit or something that a lot of our riders actually appreciate about the system. (14:55): Now, it turns out that adhering to the speed limit even without traffic sometimes is not the best thing. You have to go below the speed limit and we realize that for driving in the slopes or the gradients, in clients in San Francisco, there are many of those. The human brain is trained to, or the human drivers are sort of in subconsciously, they slow down when they go downhill in those slopes. The autonomous vehicle doesn't necessarily have to do that if it's safe and if it's staying below the speed limit. (15:31): But we learned that this is a more natural driving experience and this is what our riders would also expect in terms of the experience. So that's something that we then modify the behavior on.
turns.zh: 我不确定是否能具体指出某个方面。再说一次，这是一种整体体验，我认为必须通过许多细微之处，才能让乘客感到自然、透明和可信。我可以举一个例子，虽然在之前的讨论中可能没提到过。但由于系统设计得既谨慎又防御性，同时在没有交通的情况下也能保持适度进展，所以它永远不会超速。它不会超速，而是严格遵守限速规定——这一点深受我们许多乘客的赞赏。（14:55）：但事实证明，即使在没有交通的情况下也严格遵守限速规则有时并非最佳选择。比如在旧金山的客户群体中，很多路段都有陡坡或坡道，而人类大脑经过训练，或者说司机们下意识会放慢车速以应对下坡路况。自动驾驶车辆如果安全且保持在限速以下，则不必这样做。（15:31）：但我们发现这种更自然的驾驶体验正是乘客所期待的。因此，我们对系统行为进行了相应调整。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. I would want it to slow down. On the other hand, if I feel like I could trust that, I wish there was a button to just crazy mode, just go for it. Kind of digging a little bit into the product team's way of working, what are KPIs that you all use to track progress? I don't know, either amongst some of the teams you lead or also just broadly progress on self-driving technology. How do you know you're making progress? Is it just miles driven as something else?
turns.zh: 这说得通。我肯定希望它能减速。但另一方面，如果我觉得可以信任它，就希望能有个按钮切换到疯狂模式，放手让它去干。再深入探讨一下产品团队的工作方式，你们用来追踪进展的关键绩效指标（KPI）都有哪些？我不知道，无论是您领导的团队，还是更广泛的自动驾驶技术进展方面，如何判断是否取得了进展？是里程数之类的吗？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: There are tons of these metrics that we analyze on a daily basis, weekly basis depending upon what the metric is. But if I were to categorize them in two broad categories, that'd be the commercial and operational metrics and the system behavior metrics. So, one important thing to note here is that we're in a proof of concept or a pilot phase anymore. This is the service that we are offering to riders. Paid service in Phoenix and also it's open to public in San Francisco, so it's an actual service. (16:46): And so, we're tracking the commercial metrics in terms of the trips per week, the daily or weekly active users and all the funnel metrics that you can think of. Also, the operational metrics, the cost, right? Well, how much is the thing costing us to operate? So that's, I would say, all the stuff on the commercial scaling side. And then on the driver performance, the vehicle driver as the technology name as I alluded to earlier, the driver performance metrics, they span across safety, the compliance to the road rules, our ability to make adequate progress as in not get unduly stopped or stranded in dense traffic situations as an example.
turns.zh:
我们每天或每周都会分析大量这样的指标，具体取决于指标类型。但如果将其分为两大类，那就是商业和运营指标，以及系统行为指标。需要指出的是，我们已不再处于概念验证或试点阶段。这是我们向乘客提供的服务。在凤凰城是付费服务，在旧金山也向公众开放，所以这是一项实际服务。
（16:46）：因此，我们追踪商业指标，如每周出行次数、每日或每周活跃用户，以及您能想到的所有漏斗指标。还有运营指标，比如成本，对吧？运营成本是多少？这些都是商业扩展方面的内容。再说驾驶员表现，即我之前提到的技术名称“车辆驾驶员”相关的指标，涵盖安全性、道路规则遵守情况，以及在密集交通情况下能否正常行驶（比如不被不必要地拦停或滞留）等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are just specific metrics there? Anything you could share just like what is the actual goal in one of those teams?
turns.zh: 具体的指标有哪些？能否分享一下某个团队的实际目标？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: The goal here is to be able to drive safer than humans. Now, we don't really have one standard human driving benchmark, safety benchmark, that everybody uses, but we do gather enough of that data. We have access to enough of that data to form an opinion on or a metric on or benchmark on what does human driving look like, how many collisions, as an example, a human driver would have every a hundred thousand mile. And then we want to make sure that our performance is better than that. (18:19): So that's simplifying, right? And several things go into both calculating the benchmark as well as our performance against that benchmark. But that at the core of it, that's what we're trying to do. So that's on the safety side and then I would say on the stops and strands, which is trying to, which goes in the different direction. Hey, you can be very safe if you're not moving at all. That's not what we're building. We need to make sure that the riders get to their destination on time. So it has to be appropriately assertive and be making the right progress. (18:53): And, so again, how much did the vehicle slow down unduly, right? Or, in how many instances in a given week did it have to rely on a rescue help? Those are the situations that we want to avoid. And then, how much did we slow down the traffic for other users? So we again do extensive benchmarking and look at the priors, et cetera, and really understand would an adequate performance be there and measure our own against that.
turns.zh: 我们的目标是比人类驾驶更安全。目前，人类驾驶并没有一个通用的标准基准，但我们确实收集了大量相关数据。我们可以利用这些数据，评估人类驾驶的安全表现，比如每十万英里发生多少起碰撞事故等。然后，我们要确保自己的表现优于这个标准。（18:19）：这就是简化流程，对吧？评估基准和衡量自身表现都需要多项考量。但核心目标就是做到这一点。接下来是安全与效率的平衡。举个例子，若车辆一动不动，那当然很安全，但这不是我们的设计初衷。我们需要确保乘客能准时抵达目的地。因此，系统既要足够主动，又要确保路径规划合理。（18:53）：比如，车辆不必要减速多少次？每周有多少次需要依赖救援服务？这些都是我们希望避免的情况。另外，我们会对交通延误情况进行全面评估，参考历史数据，真正理解何种表现才算合格，并据此衡量自身表现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Today's episode is brought to you by Elements. I just recently discovered this stuff actually from another podcast and it is such sweet, salty goodness. Element is a tasty electrolyte drink mix with a science-backed electrolyte ratio. And unlike most electrolyte drinks, there's no sugar coloring, artificial ingredients, gluten or any other BS. Getting enough electrolytes helps prevent and eliminate headaches, muscle cramps, fatigue, sleeplessness and other common symptoms of electrolyte deficiency. (19:57): Element is the exclusive hydration partner to team US USA Weightlifting and many other Olympic athletes. Also, dozens of NBA and NFL teams and players rely on Element to stay hydrated along with Navy SEAL teams, FBI sniper teams and the Marines. You can try Element totally risk-free. To give it a shot, go to drinklmnt.com/lenny and you'll get a free sample pack with any purchase, which includes one packet of every flavor. (20:27): My favorite is watermelon salt. You won't find this offer publicly available, so you have to head to drinklmnt.com/lenny to take advantage of this offer. Stay salty. (20:38): I'm guessing you're not going to have an answer to when do we think we'll have fully self-driving level five autonomy. So let me ask you a different approach to that question of just what's most in the way of us getting to full self-driving where we don't have to do anything ever? Is it like miles driven? Is it like tech breakthroughs that still have to happen? Is it regulation and just cities being like, okay, it's fine. What's the biggest blocker at this point or bottleneck?
turns.zh: 太棒了。今天的节目由Elements赞助。我最近刚从另一个播客里发现了这个品牌，真是又实用又健康。Elements是一款美味的电解质饮料，科学配比电解质比例。与大多数电解质饮料不同，它不含糖、色素、人工成分、麸质等添加剂。补充充足电解质有助于预防和消除头痛、肌肉痉挛、疲劳、失眠等电解质缺乏症常见症状。（19:57）：Elements是美国举重队和众多奥运运动员的官方补水合作伙伴。此外，数十支NBA和NFL球队及球员、海军海豹突击队、FBI狙击小组等都信赖Elements保持水分平衡。现在即可免费试用，不满意可退款。访问drinklmnt.com/lenny，即可获得免费样品包，包含每种口味各一份。（20:27）：我最喜欢西瓜盐味。这优惠在公开渠道找不到，必须前往drinklmnt.com/lenny才能享受。继续保持健康吧。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: So let me share my opinion on the L5.
turns.zh: 那我来谈谈对L5的看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: So L for those who might not be very familiar with this term, L2, L3 is still very much driver assist. It gets to some level of autonomy but then it relies on the human driver at the wheel to be able to take over complex situations. L4 fully autonomous without a human driver at the wheel and no expectation of a human driver at the wheel. That's what we've been focusing on. L5 would be in any kind of road completely unstructured, off-roading in that kind of an environment, be able to drive without any map, without any priors, what have you. (21:44): And we believe that by offering the kind of service that we are offering in Phoenix and in San Francisco through the rest of this year and other cities in future is it helps realize that the dream of the fully autonomous driving, in a big way, without having to go to L5. So I think that the technology is already there. L5, I'm not sure, maybe that becomes more niche, et cetera. It solves very specific use cases. (22:16): In terms of the blocker, I would say, the technology is there, but it still needs improvements. Especially we were not able to drive in snow yet. Something that we have to tackle in future.
turns.zh: 可能对这个术语不太熟悉的朋友，L2、L3仍然属于驾驶辅助系统。它们在一定程度上实现了自动驾驶，但遇到复杂情况时，仍需人类驾驶员接管。L4则完全实现自动驾驶，无需人类驾驶员参与，且未来也不需要依赖人类接管。这一点正是我们目前重点关注的方向。L5则要在完全无路径引导的环境中实现自动驾驶，比如越野路况，甚至在没有地图和先验数据的情况下完成驾驶任务。（21:44）我们相信，通过今年在凤凰城和旧金山推出的服务，以及未来在其他城市的扩展，将有力推动实现完全自动驾驶的梦想，无需非得等到L5阶段。因此，我认为相关技术已经成熟。至于L5阶段，我不太确定，它可能更偏向于小众应用场景，专注于特定场景的解决方案。（22:16）至于技术瓶颈，我认为现有技术已基本到位，但仍需进一步改进。比如，我们目前还无法在雪地环境中正常驾驶，这正是我们未来需要攻克的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could barely drive in slow.
turns.zh: 我在雪天开车总是很吃力。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yeah. And I don't like to drive in snow. Even I, I avoid snowy days. But that is something that we still have to build as a capability in driving fully in snow now. So that's great.
turns.zh: 是啊。我不喜欢在雪天开车。就连我也尽量避开雪天出行。不过这确实是我们目前需要攻克的难题——实现完全在雪地环境中安全驾驶的能力。这很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. Clearly, there's a lot of little things, a lot of big things and it's a really interesting point about we don't need L5, L4 is great for most people. Maybe a last question along this track and then I want to pivot to a different area. So Waymo's been this long-term investment for Alphabet and many PMs often try to create buy-in and keep buy-in for large investment and large project. I know this is a different scale of investment than what most PMs work through. But is there anything you've learned about keeping leaders bought in and excited and continuing to invest in a project for years and years? Specifically just like tactics that keep people excited and bought into a long-term investment?
turns.zh: 有道理。显然，技术难点有很多，大到整体架构，小到细节处理。关于L5阶段的讨论很有意思。显然，L4阶段对大多数人来说已经足够了。最后再问一个相关问题，然后我要转向另一个话题。Waymo一直是Alphabet的长期投资项目，许多项目经理经常需要争取支持并维持对大型投资和项目的关注。我知道这项投资的规模远超大多数项目经理所面对的。但在让领导者持续投入并保持热情、持续多年为项目注资方面，您有哪些心得？特别是如何激发人们对长期投资的热情并保持投入？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yeah. So first of all, we are fortunate that we have the backing from Alphabet and other investors. And the autonomous vehicle industry is interesting and I think the last year has been interesting with more consolidation happening. So I think the name of the game here is to show progress, show meaningful progress and meaningful progress, not just in terms of technology but in terms of commercial deployments. That is the rubber meets the road, if you will, phase off of the product. (23:54): And the results have to speak for themselves, for our investors to have the confidence in us. So notwithstanding what's happening to other AB companies in the industry, it's about what we are doing. And then look at the progress that we've been making and where we are headed. And the fact that we've been accelerating our milestones and going through our own expectations, I think, these are very positive signals to our investors as well. (24:23): Another startup as well, t's not about you have to do what's the right thing for the business. Your focus is on creating value for the customers, creating value for the riders. You have to build a business that makes sense and the investors see that too. Or we're not going to do something unnatural or something that doesn't align with the business goals in order to gain any short term brownie points with investors. I think it doesn't work that way and the investors will see through that too. (24:52): Definitely Alphabet has been our backer for forever. So, it's really about focusing on building the right business and doing the right thing for the users.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，我们很幸运能得到Alphabet和其他投资者的支持。自动驾驶汽车行业很有趣，我认为过去一年的整合进程令人瞩目。所以关键在于展示进展，展现有意义的进步——不仅是技术层面的，更是商业应用层面的。这就像是产品落地阶段的关键考验。（23:54）：而结果必须能说服投资者对我们保持信心。尽管行业内其他自动驾驶公司面临种种挑战，但我们专注于自身的行动。回顾我们取得的进展以及未来的发展方向，持续超越既定里程碑并超越自身预期，这些都是向投资者传递积极信号的重要举措。（24:23）：作为另一家初创公司，关键在于你必须做对业务发展有利的事。你的核心任务是为客户创造价值，为乘客创造价值。你必须构建一个合理的商业模式，投资者也会看重这一点。我们不会为了短期取悦投资者而做出违背商业目标的举动。我认为这种做法不可取，投资者也会看透这一点。（24:52）：Alphabet始终是我们的坚实后盾。因此，关键在于专注于构建正确的商业模式，为用户创造价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's a great takeaway that if you're finding that there's a buy-in and continued support for what you're building, focus on momentum and showing success. It's pretty simple if you think about it. And it's hard to cut something that's just showing success. And so, even at the scale of Waymo, it's a great lesson. So that makes sense.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个重要的启示：如果你发现人们对你的项目有认同感并持续支持，那么就专注于保持势头并展示成功。说起来很简单，但要做到却很难。即便像Waymo这样规模的公司，也能从中汲取宝贵经验。所以这确实很有道理。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We talked a bit about other companies you've worked at and so I want to kind of zoom out a little bit. And I just want to ask, you worked at Amazon, Cisco, Waymo now, startup you mentioned. What are just some of the biggest lessons you've learned about building successful teams and successful products?
turns.zh: 我们之前谈到过你曾就职的其他公司，现在我想稍微拓宽一下视野。我想问，你曾在亚马逊、思科、Waymo工作，现在又提到初创公司。你在构建成功团队和产品方面学到的最重要经验是什么？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: In terms of the product, whether you're working for a big company or a startup, the core product management tenant is still the same, which is, you have to work backwards from the customer problem or the user problem. Building a technology for the sake of it doesn't really go that far, so you really have to focus on the, what are you building, who are you building it for and what problem are you solving? (26:05): And this applies in any context. And Amazon has this great process where the PMs have to write a press release for the finished product even before they start building the product. That's the first thing that they have to do is to write that press release like the product is about to launch today. What are you telling the users about that product? Really forces them to think about the value proposition more thoroughly. (26:33): And I know many other companies are starting to look at that practice as well, but I find it very effective.
turns.zh: 就产品而言，无论是在大公司还是初创公司工作，核心的产品管理原则都是一致的：你必须从客户或用户的问题出发进行反向设计。为了技术而开发技术往往走不远，因此你必须专注于：你在开发什么产品？为谁开发？要解决什么问题？（26:05）：这适用于任何场景。亚马逊有一个很棒的流程，产品经理甚至在开始开发产品之前就必须为最终产品撰写新闻稿。这是他们必须做的第一件事——就好像产品今天就要发布一样。他们要向用户传达什么？这真的迫使他们更深入地思考价值主张。（26:33）：我知道许多其他公司也开始借鉴这种做法，但我发现它非常有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you do that at Waymo or do you folks do that? Is there kind of a system there or?
turns.zh: Waymo会这样做吗？你们有这样的体系吗？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: The explicit PR FAQ process that Amazon follows is, I think, Waymo has its own version of it. But it is about sort of focusing on the customer problem. Now, Waymo is also a very different kind of product. It's highly integrated. And different types of product management flavors, if you will. Some are more technically focused and technically deep, some are more commercially focused. So they all adapt. They have their versions of working backwards from the customer problem. But that still remains the core tenant in my mind. (27:13): The other big lesson, at least working in some of the large companies that I have had is it's also very important to know what you're not building. And this one is not only in big companies, I would say even in startups, it's extremely important to know what you're not building because you could very easily get swayed by customer X telling you to do this, customer y telling you to do that. And a product that tries to be all things to all people usually doesn't end up going anywhere. (27:42): So that focus, that prioritization and being crisp about what you're building and what you're not building is very important. And then, in the context of the large companies, what I was going to say was, I think, is the classic innovator's dilemma. The large companies tend to be the market share leaders in their focus areas. And so, the product team and the product leaders can get very incremental in their product strategy and then lo and behold, you see an upstart that comes and disrupts them. (28:16): And so, I have definitely learned the lesson that you need to disrupt yourself before somebody else does because it's going to happen. It's inevitable. And large companies that are constantly challenging themselves and disrupting their own models or their own product capabilities to bring those, even something more transformational for the customers, are the ones that really succeed. And I think this is where the product leaders have to bring in that mindset of, hey, are we getting too complacent or it's time to just.
turns.zh: 亚马逊遵循的明确产品经理FAQ流程，我认为Waymo也有自己的版本。但关键在于要聚焦客户需求。如今，Waymo也是一款截然不同的产品。它高度集成化。产品管理风格也各不相同，有的更偏重技术，有的更侧重商业化。因此，各团队需因地制宜，开发出适合自身的客户需求倒推式产品战略。但在我看来，这仍是核心要义。（27:13）：另一个重要经验——至少在我服务过的大型公司中如此——就是要清楚自己不该做什么。这不仅适用于大公司，对初创企业同样重要。毕竟，客户X要求你做这个，客户Y要求你做那个，你很容易被带偏。试图面面俱到的产品通常走不远。（27:42）：因此，专注、优先排序以及清晰界定产品边界至关重要。就大型公司而言，我想说这就是经典的"创新者困境"。大公司往往是所在领域的市场领导者，因此产品团队和负责人可能会在产品战略上变得过于保守。结果呢？某个初创公司突然闯入，彻底颠覆了他们。（28:16）：所以我深刻领悟到：你必须在别人动手前就自我颠覆，因为这不可避免。那些不断挑战自我、不断突破自身模式或产品能力、甚至为客户带来变革性体验的大公司，才能真正成功。我认为这就需要产品负责人树立这样的思维：嘿，我们是否变得过于自满了？是时候行动了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good reminder. Is there an example of you doing that or something you worked on where you got the company to commit to something that maybe could have been a threat from a disruptor or maybe even just seen that happening at a company? Just like is there a specific project or investment that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 这真是很好的提醒。你能举个例子吗？比如你做过什么项目，让公司下定决心投入资源，避免被颠覆者威胁，或者预见了某家公司可能面临的颠覆？有没有具体的项目或投资案例？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: [NEW_PARAGRAPH]At Amazon, I was the first PM and then I drove the team around it for a no-code application development platform called Honey Code. So that was a brand new service. Amazon had never delved in that space before. It was more infrastructure focused and this was first of its kind service that the team worked on. And this has played out many times in my career, and so I am a big believer in disrupting yourself before somebody else does it.
turns.zh: [新段落]在亚马逊，我是首位产品经理，负责领导团队开发无代码应用开发平台Honey Code。这是一个全新的服务，亚马逊此前从未涉足该领域。当时亚马逊更专注于基础设施，而这个团队打造的服务开创了先河。这种模式在我的职业生涯中多次奏效，因此我坚信，要想在别人动手前就自我颠覆，才是明智之举。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think is the most underrated PM skill that you suggest people, maybe especially early in their career, that they should focus on maybe that they're probably not thinking about?
turns.zh: 你认为最被低估的产品经理技能是什么？你建议初入职场的人尤其应该关注什么？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I think the listening and empathy are the top ones. These are very important because I think when folks think about product management, they think about the influencing without authority and prioritization and being able to write with PR, et cetera, all those things are sort of more top of mind. The listening and empathy, I wouldn't say that they are underrated, I think is there's now a lot more recognition that these are sort of core skills if you want to be able to influence a lot without authority. But I think it's easier said than done. You really have to come in with that growth mindset, with that beginner's mindset, be able to absorb and just learn and listen and don't jump in with ideas necessarily, right? Take the time to formulate that opinion to really learn and understand the customer and the market and really be true to that tenant of working backwards from the customer problem, not just say because it's become such a platitude now in the product world.
turns.zh: 我认为倾听和同理心是最重要的两项技能。这两项能力至关重要，因为当人们想到产品管理时，往往会联想到"无权影响他人却能达成目标"、"优先处理事务"、"善于与公关团队合作"等传统观念。然而，倾听和同理心并未被充分重视，如今人们越来越意识到，若想在无权施加影响的情况下有效发挥作用，这些核心技能必不可少。但说起来容易做起来难。你需要秉持成长型思维，保持初学者心态，善于吸收知识、倾听他人意见，不急于强加自己的想法。花时间形成自己的观点，深入理解客户和市场需求，真正践行"从客户问题出发反向设计产品"的理念——毕竟这已成为产品界的陈词滥调。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's a book. There's a whole book called Working Backwards now.
turns.zh: 是的，有一本书。现在有一本完整的《反向设计》（Working Backwards）。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yes. That is the one thing that I would say that somebody who's starting out as a product manager really try to follow that principle. And then listening and empathy is going to go a long way in terms of being able to do that.
turns.zh: 没错。对于刚入行的产品经理，我会建议他们务必遵循这一原则。倾听和同理心在实现这一目标的过程中也将发挥重要作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On listening and empathy, what do you think helped you most develop those two skills?
turns.zh: 谈到倾听和同理心，你认为哪项技能对你的成长帮助最大？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: So I think for me, part of it was just doing this over and over again in different environments, in different product launches that I have led in different types of companies that I've worked with. In startup as well as big company, the dynamic is different. And, again, the team that you're working with in different companies have a different culture. So, when you're working with let's say an engineering leader, being able to understand what are his or her constraints? Where is he or she coming from? What does impact look like to that person? And then understanding where you're aligned, where you're not aligned are things that you have to develop and start paying a lot more attention to as you rise in your career or go up the ladder. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And I think a lot of that for me came by just being in different kind of situations and different kind of environments.
turns.zh: 对我而言，关键在于反复实践。无论是在不同公司领导的产品发布会，还是在初创企业与大公司中工作，环境各不相同。与不同团队合作时，团队文化也存在差异。比如，面对工程团队负责人，你需要理解其工作限制、出发点以及对影响力的定义。只有不断磨练这些能力，随着职业晋升才能真正领悟其中的真谛。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That's what I often say also, a lot of this just comes from doing it again and again and again. There's not going to take a course and then just I'm a great listener, I'm done.
turns.zh: 是的。这也是我常说的——很多能力都需要通过反复实践才能掌握。没有哪门课程能让你一夜之间成为出色的倾听者或同理者。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yeah, no, it doesn't. Lenny (32:19) Yeah, which is not easy to ... It'd be nice if there's a book you read and then you become a great listener and a great empathizer.
turns.zh: 确实不行。莱尼（32:19）是啊，这可不容易。要是真有本能书读一读就能成为优秀的倾听者和同理者，那就太好了。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Well, I think one take or one that I could share is just challenging your own assumptions. So, I think listening with an open mind but then are you proactively trying to challenge your own assumptions is extremely important. As a big enough product manager as well as a seasoned product leader, if you're not doing enough of that, then I think you might not be listening well, right? Or you might not be picking on the cues. If there's no conflict, if there's no contention, then something is missing.
turns.zh: 我认为关键在于挑战自己的假设。带着开放心态倾听的同时，主动质疑自己的认知，这至关重要。无论是资深产品经理还是经验丰富的领导者，如果做得不够，那说明你的倾听能力不足，或者没能捕捉到关键信息。若沟通毫无摩擦、毫无争执，那说明信息传递出了偏差。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's not often you're going to be always right.
turns.zh: 人们很少能永远正确。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one more question along these lines. You've been promoted many times, now you're in a place where you promote people and I'm curious for someone that maybe wants to get promoted or struggling to get promoted, what would you say are probably the reasons they aren't? Or what do you think people should focus on if they want to just get a promotion and many promotions in their career?
turns.zh: 或许再问一个相关的问题。你多次获得晋升，现在你处于一个负责提拔他人的职位。我很好奇那些可能想获得晋升或正为晋升而努力的人，他们不被晋升的原因可能是什么？或者说，如果想在职业生涯中多次晋升，人们应该关注哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I'm going to say something that might sound a little cheeky, but I think the way to get promoted is to not want it too badly. It is about you have to focus on the impact. It's about having an impact and then doing what is right for the business. So not sort of optimizing things for your promotion, which look, we are all ambitious human beings. And there's nothing wrong with wanting a promotion, just to be clear, and there's nothing wrong with being ambitious, but then focus on the impact. (34:03): Are you working on the right things that will have the right outcome for the business? Because if you are and if you are giving it to your 100%, that will be visible. And making your ambitions known to your manager, to your leader, is a good thing that you should. And so, when the right opportunity comes, at least your leader or manager is aware that, hey, this person wanted to work on something more challenging, so maybe I put her on that project. But you have to be focused on really creating the right impact for the company and not optimizing for yourself to get promoted. If you try to maneuver that too much, it becomes visible and it's not a positive signal to the organization when they can see that that's what you're trying to do. And it also distracts you from the things that you need to be focusing on. So, I would say, improve your skillset as a product manager. Make sure that you're made your vision known that you want to work on challenging high visibility projects or products that really test or stretch your skills and then be really dedicated to that cause and work on what has the business impact for the company, do the right things.
turns.zh: 我要说点可能听起来有点冒犯的话，但我认为获得晋升的关键在于别太执着于晋升本身。关键在于你必须专注于产生影响。首先要创造影响，然后做对业务有利的事。别为了晋升而优化一切——我们都是有抱负的人，想获得晋升本无可厚非，追求上进也无可指责，但重点应放在创造真正的影响上。（34:03）：你是否在做对业务有益的事？因为如果你做了，如果你全力以赴，成果自然会显现。向你的经理或领导透露你的晋升意愿是件好事，这样当合适的机会出现时，他们至少会知道你渴望挑战更具挑战性的项目。然后，当合适的机会出现时，至少你的领导或经理会知道，嘿，这个人想做更有挑战性的项目，所以也许我会把她安排到那个项目中。但你必须专注于为公司创造真正的影响，而不是为了晋升而优化一切。如果你在这方面操之过急，组织会察觉到，这可不是个积极的信号，而且还会让你偏离真正需要关注的重点。所以，我建议提升你的产品经理技能。确保你让别人清楚你的愿景——你想参与具有挑战性、高可见度的项目或产品，这些项目或产品能真正考验或提升你的技能，然后全身心投入到对公司有影响力的事业中去，做好正确的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that advice. I 100% agree with all of that. I have a couple final Waymo questions and then we're going to get to our very exciting lightning round. Just for folks that maybe want to try out Waymo, so maybe just like where's it live now? When do you think it'll roll out to new cities? And then, how do people try it and use it if they live in one of those cities? If that's possible.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个建议。我完全赞同。我还有几个关于Waymo的最终问题，之后我们将进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。对于那些可能想尝试Waymo的人来说，Waymo目前在哪里？你认为它何时会扩展到新城市？如果住在这些城市的人想尝试或使用Waymo服务，该怎么做？如果可能的话。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: We are already in the Phoenix metro area and in San Francisco. So in those cities you can just go and download the app and you can use the service. We have done initial fully autonomous testing in LA. And we're going to be expanding in LA through the rest of the year, so stay tuned for more development on that front. And then, we do have a list of cities that we're going to be rolling out in the coming years, but unfortunately, I can't share that list just as yet.
turns.zh: 我们已经在凤凰城大都会区和旧金山运营。所以在这些城市，你只需下载应用程序即可使用服务。我们在洛杉矶进行了初步的全自动测试。今年剩余时间内，我们将在洛杉矶继续扩展业务，敬请期待后续进展。然后，我们确实有未来几年要扩展到的城市列表，但很遗憾，目前我还不能透露这些城市名单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And if someone lives in one of those cities, is there a way they could try to get on a wait list or try to use this stuff or is it closed doors right now?
turns.zh: 如果有人住在这些城市之一，是否有办法加入等待名单或尝试使用这些服务，还是目前还不开放？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: So it is open doors in San Francisco and Phoenix.
turns.zh: 所以在旧金山和凤凰城是开放的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So you just sign up and you get on the waitlist and then you might get off?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以你只需注册，然后加入等待名单，之后可能会被选中？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: In Phoenix, I don't even think that there is a wait list.
turns.zh: 在凤凰城，我甚至觉得那里根本没有等候名单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: On the waitlist.
turns.zh: 在等候名单上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got to move to Phoenix. That's cool.
turns.zh: 我得搬去凤凰城了。那挺酷的。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Or just wait, just yeah, a little while in San Francisco. But yeah, Phoenix is great. So, if you want to move there, that's totally fine.
turns.zh: 或者就再等等吧，在旧金山再待一阵子。不过凤凰城确实很棒。所以，如果你想搬过去，那完全没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I'm going to start packing tonight. Just joking. Anything else you want to touch on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 不，我今晚就开始收拾行李了。开玩笑的。在我们进入超级激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想聊的吗？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: No, I think we talked about a bunch of things. It's been a great conversation so far.
turns.zh: 没有了，我觉得我们已经聊了很多了。到目前为止，这次对话非常棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's not over yet. We've reached our very exciting lightning round. I have six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 还没结束呢。我们现在要进入超级激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Bring it on.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, here we go. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Crossing The Chasm by Geoffrey Moore and Clayton Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma are still sort of the two classics in product management that I have quoted a lot and I have recommended to many folks.
turns.zh: 杰弗里·摩尔的《跨越鸿沟》和克莱顿·克里斯滕森的《创新者的困境》仍然是我在产品管理领域经常引用并推荐给很多人的两本经典著作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I've got both in my little bookshelf behind me.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我把它们都放在我身后的小书架上了。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yeah, me too.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I have an eight-year-old daughter, so my viewing choices are very much influenced by what she watches. But let's see, I did enjoy the Top Gun, the new Top Gun movie, Top Gun Maverick quite a bit. We watched it in the theater and visuals were just fantastic. I think it was also inspiring to see what Tom Cruise was able to do and it's quite a feat that he pulled off at this age. It was very inspirational.
turns.zh: 我有个八岁的女儿，所以我的观影选择很大程度上受她喜好的影响。不过说起来，我确实很喜欢《壮志凌云》——新版的《壮志凌云：独行侠》。我们在影院看的，视觉效果简直太棒了。我觉得看汤姆·克鲁斯能做到这些，真的很鼓舞人心。他这个年纪还能完成这些动作，真是了不起，太令人敬佩了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fully agree. Favorite interview question that you like to ask people?
turns.zh: 完全赞同。你最喜欢问别人的采访问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Especially at the senior levels, I always ask them, when was one time that you failed and what did you learn from it? I've seen that folks who has either say that they've never failed or they're trying a success story as a failure story are usually, they're disingenuous or have not had the depth of experience. So I ask that question and I'm looking for some real solid examples there.
turns.zh: 特别是面对高管时，我总会问他们：你什么时候失败过？从中学到了什么？我发现那些说自己从不失败，或者把成功故事包装成失败故事的人，往往要么不够真诚，要么经验不够丰富。所以我会问这个问题，希望能听到真实的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What's a favorite recent product that you've discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你最近发现了什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I wouldn't say that I recently discovered it. It's on my wishlist to buy very soon. I'm all for sustainable mobility, so I am shopping for a foldable ebike so I can do more mountain biking without doing mountain biking. That's the sustainable part for me, I guess.
turns.zh: 我倒不算最近才发现的。不过它在我的购物清单上，很快就会买了。我一直支持可持续出行，所以我在挑选一款可折叠的电动自行车，这样我就能在不实际骑山地车的情况下体验更多山地骑行的乐趣。这对我来说就是可持续出行的一部分吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a specific model or brand that you are most excited about?
turns.zh: 有没有特别让你心动的具体型号或品牌？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I would take recommendations from you, but I'm still shopping. I think electric, there are a couple.
turns.zh: 我倒是想听听你的推荐，但我还在挑选中。电动车方面，有几款挺不错的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Folks who have recommendations, leave suggestions in the comments.
turns.zh: 好的。有推荐的朋友，可以在评论区留言。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Please do.
turns.zh: 麻烦啦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what's something relatively minor you've changed in your team's product development process that you've found has had a tremendous impact?
turns.zh: 还有一件相对较小的改进，你在团队产品开发流程中做过的，却产生了巨大的影响？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: I wouldn't say that this is a product development process, although, in different parts of phase of my career, I have definitely instituted different types of processes and tools that have helped improve the product development. But I would give you an interesting one that I use a lot in my prior company and then I use a different form of it here in Waymo is what I used to call as the rule of seven. If there have been seven emails in an email thread and you still haven't resolved the issue, just call the person or get in a room huddle, resolve it live. (39:43): But the long email exchanges that don't converge and go anywhere I feel are a waste of time for many people. So I'm like, you've got to a limit. Waymo is a bigger company, so the limit's more like 10, but if you haven't resolved something within an X number of emails, please just get on a call, get in a room and get it resolved.
turns.zh: 我不会说这算是一种产品开发流程，不过，在我职业生涯的不同阶段，我确实推行过不同类型的流程和工具，帮助提升了产品开发效率。但我要分享一个我在前公司常用、如今在Waymo也有所改进的有趣方法——我称之为“七次法则”。如果一封邮件往来超过七轮邮件，仍未解决问题，那就直接打电话或开个会议当场解决。（39:43）：但我觉得那些漫长却毫无进展的邮件往来实在是浪费大家的时间。所以我觉得必须设个限。Waymo是大公司，所以限制数字是10封，但如果超过这个数量仍未解决问题，就直接打电话或开会解决。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And the idea is it's seven if it's like you and that person going back and forth seven times?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这个规则是说，如果是你和对方来回沟通七次吗？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yeah. Or all of people are just going back and forth. And then adding more people and then everybody chime in, but where is this thing really headed?
turns.zh: 对。或者所有人都在来回沟通。然后再加入更多人讨论，但最终方向还是不明朗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Final question. If anyone gets to ride in a Waymo, what's a pro tip for them to have an awesome experience?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个主意。最后一个问题。如果有人有机会乘坐Waymo的自动驾驶车，你能给他们一个享受绝佳体验的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Bring your favorite playlist, sit back and enjoy the ride.
turns.zh: 带上你最喜欢的播放列表，坐下来享受旅程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. When I was on my right, I turned on some jazz and it was raining outside. It was real cozy.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我之前乘坐Waymo时，打开了爵士乐频道，当时外面还在下雨。真的很惬意。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: But did you actually do it on the ... So, so there's a feature, if you have a Google, you have to download the Google Assistant, but you can actually play your playlist list in the car.
turns.zh: 但你实际上是在车里操作的吗？所以，有个功能，如果你有谷歌账号，就得下载谷歌助手，但实际上你可以在车里播放播放列表。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's cool. No, I chose a station that was in there just like jazz music.
turns.zh: 太酷了。不，我选了一个车载的爵士乐电台。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Okay. Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. This is great. All right. Hopefully I get another ride someday.
turns.zh: 是的。好的。这太棒了。好的，我希望以后还有机会体验。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Yes, you should.
turns.zh: 是的，你应该去试试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shweta, this was amazing. I am going to start packing my bags for Phoenix. I'm going to sell my car. Everything's going to change
turns.zh: Shweta，这次交流太棒了。我要开始收拾行李去凤凰城了。我要卖掉我的车。一切都要改变了。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Exactly what we wish for.
turns.zh: 这正是我们所期望的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's your KPI. Thank you again for being here. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they want to learn more, reach out, ask you maybe some questions, maybe apply to join Waymo if you're hiring, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 这就是你的关键绩效指标（KPI）。再次感谢你今天的到来。最后两个问题，如果人们想了解更多信息、联系你、提问，或者申请加入Waymo（如果有招聘的话），该去哪里找你？他们又如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: You can find me on LinkedIn. And then if you are interested in opportunities at Waymo, go to Waymo career web page. You should see all the open positions. It's okay for you to reach out to me on LinkedIn as well for product management roles. How can listeners be useful to me? I would say, hey, sign up for the ride in Phoenix or San Francisco and LA when we open up, give us feedback.
turns.zh: 你可以在LinkedIn上找到我。如果你对Waymo的机会感兴趣，可以访问Waymo的招聘页面。你应该能看到所有开放职位。也可以在LinkedIn上联系我，申请产品管理职位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Shweta, thank you again for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Shweta，再次感谢你的到来。

turns.speaker: Shweta Shrivastava
turns.en: Thank you. It was great to have this conversation.
turns.zh: 谢谢。很高兴能与大家交流。
